results.authors: Montalban X, Lebrun-Frenay C, Oh J, et al.
results.key_findings: Five regions for dissemination in space (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve). The optic nerve can be shown by MRI, OCT or VEP. The kappa free light chain index is accepted alongside CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands. The central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions are supporting MRI markers.
results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria

results.authors: Wattjes MP, Ciccarelli O, Reich DS, et al.
results.key_findings: Diagnostic MRI should include the brain with 3D FLAIR, T2 and pre- and post-gadolinium T1, and the spinal cord with at least two sagittal sequences, ideally in the same session.
results.title: 2021 MAGNIMS-CMSC-NAIMS consensus recommendations on the use of MRI in patients with multiple sclerosis

output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) adds the optic nerve as a fifth region, accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed. In people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, additional supporting evidence is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not label this a clinically isolated syndrome: the right leg sensory episode 9 months ago left objective signs (right Babinski sign, right leg vibration and touch loss) and is a second attack
Do not start a DMT before NMOSD and MOGAD are excluded; some MS treatments (natalizumab, fingolimod, interferon-beta) can worsen NMOSD
Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF (here periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord and left optic nerve: five regions, so no separate DIT is required).

Offer high-dose methylprednisolone for the disabling left optic neuritis (acuity 20/80): oral 500 mg daily for 5 days or, as an inpatient, IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days; advise her to avoid naproxen during the course or add a proton pump inhibitor; consider plasma exchange if severe visual loss does not respond.

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (two attacks in 9 months, enhancing optic nerve and periventricular lesions, lesions in 5 of 5 regions), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception.

Before starting disease-modifying therapy, check full blood count with lymphocyte count, liver function, HBsAg and anti-HBc, hepatitis C and VZV IgG (HIV already non-reactive), and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before treatment starts
Supplement vitamin D for the low 25-OH level (13 ng/mL) as general health advice, and explain the heat-related transient worsening she reports (Uhthoff phenomenon).

key_clinical_evidence: Day-5 painful left optic neuritis (acuity 20/80, left RAPD, red desaturation, mild disc swelling) with an enhancing swollen 10 mm intraorbital segment of the left optic nerve and a prolonged left P100 (132 ms).

Two attacks with objective evidence: the current optic neuritis and a right leg sensory attack 9 months ago that left a right Babinski sign and right leg vibration and touch loss, matched by the right dorsolateral C4-C5 lesion.

DIS: 5 of 5 regions: periventricular (ovoid and callososeptal lesions, open-ring enhancing left lesion), juxtacortical (right parietal, left frontal), infratentorial (right middle cerebellar peduncle), spinal cord (C4-C5, T5-T6), optic nerve (left). With five regions no separate DIT or CSF is needed; enhancing and non-enhancing lesions also coexist.
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay, short peripheral cord lesions and five CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (kFLC index 17.9) argue against NMOSD and MOGAD despite the disc swelling.
Low 25-OH vitamin D (13 ng/mL) is a risk factor and comorbidity; it does not explain the lesions.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Priya Nair is a 29-year-old right-handed South Asian woman who presents to the neurology inpatient service with a 5-day history of progressive painful blurring of vision in her left eye. She first noticed a mild ache behind her left eye four evenings ago, which she initially attributed to prolonged screen time. The following morning she observed that her vision in the left eye was blurry and that colors appeared dull and desaturated when she covered her right eye. The pain behind the left eye worsened with upward and lateral gaze movements. Over the subsequent three days her visual acuity in the left eye continued to decline to the point that she could not read text on her phone with the left eye alone. She also noticed that the pain woke her from sleep on one occasion. She presented to her primary care physician who noted a left afferent pupillary defect and referred her urgently to the emergency department. On further questioning, she recalls a distinct episode approximately 9 months ago in which she developed progressive numbness and a pins-and-needles sensation in her right leg from mid-thigh to the foot over the course of one week. The symptoms persisted for about 4 weeks before gradually improving. She was seen at an urgent care clinic where lumbar disc herniation was suspected; no imaging was performed. She now notes that she still has faint residual tingling in the right foot when she is fatigued or overheated, but the episode was otherwise felt to have resolved. She denies any prior episodes of vision loss, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, limb weakness, or bowel and bladder dysfunction. She denies recent fevers, rash, joint pain, oral ulcers, genital ulcers, Raynaud phenomenon, or recent viral illness. She has not traveled internationally and denies tick exposures.

neurological_exam.additional: Lhermitte sign negative. No meningismus. Patient reports that the residual right foot tingling returns transiently when she is overheated (Uhthoff phenomenon). EDSS estimated at 2.5.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin intact bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual acuity right eye 20/20, left eye 20/80. Left relative afferent pupillary defect present (Marcus Gunn pupil). Red desaturation in the left eye: red appears markedly washed-out compared with the right eye. Fundoscopy: mild left optic disc swelling without pallor; right disc normal. Visual fields: generalized reduction of sensitivity in the left eye on confrontation, right eye full. CN III-IV-VI: extraocular movements full and conjugate; no diplopia; no nystagmus. CN V: facial sensation intact bilaterally. CN VII: no facial asymmetry. CN VIII: hearing grossly intact bilaterally. CN IX-X: palate elevates symmetrically. CN XII: tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal casual gait. Tandem gait mildly uncertain but no frank ataxia. Romberg sign negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. Speech fluent without dysarthria. Language comprehension and repetition intact. Attention intact. Affect anxious but cooperative.
neurological_exam.motor: Upper extremities: 5/5 strength bilaterally in deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, finger extensors, and interossei. No pronator drift. Lower extremities: 5/5 strength bilaterally in hip flexors, knee extensors and flexors, ankle dorsiflexors, and plantar flexors. No atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally. Triceps 2+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 3+ bilaterally. Achilles 3+ bilaterally. Right plantar response extensor (Babinski sign positive). Left plantar response flexor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Decreased vibration sense in the right lower extremity from the knee distally (residual from prior episode, compared with left which is intact).
